extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, law students, and practitioners handling patent litigation/pleadings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on pleading, parties, defenses, and evidentiary notice in actions for patent infringement at law (how to draft a declaration, who may sue, and what defenses may be pleaded or must be noticed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must particularly describe and ascertain invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor shall particularly describe and ascertain the nature of his invention, and in what manner the same is to be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere announcement of an idea (e.g., 'apply heated air to a furnace') is not sufficient; the specification must include enough detail or a mechanical illustration to show how to perform the invention (illustrated by Neilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle eo nomine not patentable; embodiment may be
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle co nomine (mere enunciation of a proposition or fact) is not patentable; but the principle of the invention embodied in a practical form may be secured to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish between an abstract law/principle (not patentable) and its practical embodiment; claims that effectively claim only a principle will fail, whereas claims that describe practical means to apply the principle may be valid (Neilson and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration must show title with convenient certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration in an action for infringement should show a title in the plaintiff with convenient certainty and set forth all matters of the essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without these allegations the plaintiff fails to show a legal right to judgment. The declaration should be considered in its parts and must affirm facts essential to the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averment that plaintiff was original and first inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should commence with a recital that the plaintiff was 'the original and first inventor' of the subject-matter complained of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This averment is necessary even though the letters-patent are prima facie evidence; the fact must appear affirmatively at trial, so it must be alleged in the pleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averment that the invention was new, useful, and not on sale or public use before application
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should aver the subject-matter was 'new and useful', 'not known or used before the plaintiff's invention or discovery', and 'not at the time of his application for a patent in public use or on sale with his consent or allowance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are essential elements of the plaintiff's title and must be pleaded to support a claim for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averment that patent obtained in due form
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to aver that the plaintiff, being the original and first inventor, obtained letters-patent for his invention in due form of law, under the seal of the patent office, signed by the Secretary of State, and countersigned by the Commissioner of Patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formerly patents bore different attestations, but the pleading must allege issuance in the form prescribed by law so courts may presume preliminary steps were properly taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set forth substance of the grant and profert of letters-patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of the grant should be set forth: that the letters-patent secured to the plaintiff the exclusive right for the term (e.g., fourteen years), and the invention should be briefly described as set forth in the letters-patent, of which profert should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to include the full specification in the declaration; the defendant may obtain the specification by praying oyer and it will then form part of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration should aver value of patent right, breach, and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration is concluded by an averment of the value of the patent right and of the breach by the defendant, and the damages sustained by the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grounds the relief sought and quantifies the injury alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements when plaintiff sues as assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff sues in the character of assignee, he must set forth both the patentee's title and his own, and should aver that the assignments were duly recorded in the patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission to state recording may be cured by verdict if otherwise sufficient; proof of recording may be given at trial, and assignments may be recorded after suit but before trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may bring suit (parties) — patentees, assignees, grantees of exclusive rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The action shall be brought in the name(s) of the person(s) interested, whether as patentee, assignees, or as grantees of the exclusive right within a specified part of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grantee for a particular district may bring suit in his own name in that district; assignees of whole interest must sue in assignee's name; undivided-part assignments require joint names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where assignment of whole interest exists, action only in assignee's name; undivided part requires joint names
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee has assigned his whole interest, the action can only be brought in the name of the assignee; where assignment is of an undivided part of the interest, the action should be brought in the joint names of the patentee and the assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assignment only agreed to be made (not yet made), the action should be in the name of the patentee; assignment may be recorded any time after suit and before trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading options: special plea vs general issue with notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may plead specially, or plead the general issue ('not guilty') and give notice in writing of special matters he intends to put in evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory notice regime was implemented to avoid pleading difficulties and to protect plaintiffs from surprise; pleading specially provides the notice itself, while pleading general issue requires separate written notice of special matters when those matters are to be relied on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 15 special matters requiring 30-day written notice when general issue pleaded
rubrics_metrics.description: When pleading the general issue, the defendant may give the statute in evidence and certain special matters (with 30 days' written notice) including: that the specification does not contain the whole truth or contains more than necessary to produce the effect (concealment/addition to deceive); that the patentee was not the original and first inventor of the thing patented or a substantial part thereof; that it had been described in some public work anterior to the patentee's discovery; that it had been in public use or on sale with his consent before application; or that he surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These matters, if proved, can be dispositive and historically led to judgment for defendant; the statute's list is not exhaustive of all possible defenses but identifies matters requiring notice when the general issue is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: When relying on prior use/knowledge, notice must state names, residences, and where used
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant relies on the fact of a previous invention, knowledge, or use of the thing patented, he shall state in his notice the names and places of residence of those he intends to prove had prior knowledge and where the same thing had been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was added to require specification of the particulars of asserted prior use and to prevent overly vague notices; courts construe notices strictly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice must be strictly construed (geographic and factual limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of special matter must be strictly construed; if the defendant gives notice he will prove prior use 'in the United States' he cannot then offer evidence of prior use in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularity in the notice is important; failing to specify limits may prevent admission of evidence outside those bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses provable under general issue without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the general issue, without notice, the defendant may show that he never did the act complained of (no infringement), that he acted under a license or purchase, that the plaintiff is an alien not entitled to a patent, that the plaintiff lacks title as assignee, or that the patent was not duly issued (e.g., defective signatures/seal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are ordinary factual or formal defenses that the defendant may introduce without complying with the statutory notice requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense that subject is not a patentable category (not art/machine/manufacture/composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitting novelty, the defendant may show the invention is not an 'art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter' in the sense of the statute (i.e., not a patentable subject-matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from want of novelty (which is a statutory defense requiring notice when pleaded under general issue) and may be raised under the general issue without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of lack of utility/worthlessness may be shown without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show that, though new, the invention fails in point of utility and is worthless and frivolous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of utility is a clear bar to the action and can be raised under the general issue without the statutory notice requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense that specification is ambiguous or unintelligible (patent void for ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show there is no specification, or that the specification is so ambiguous and unintelligible that the court cannot determine from it what the invention is intended to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear and distinct specification is essential to validity; ambiguity that prevents ascertainment of the patentee's monopoly renders the patent void for ambiguity and is put in issue by the plea of 'not guilty' (different from the statutory concealment/addition issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of object, means, and end when principle is well known
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the principle is well known but the inventor applies it, courts consider the object with which, the means by which, and the end for which the application takes place to determine whether invention exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where the law of natural science is known, the patentability turns on whether the application (object, means, and end) is sufficiently inventive or merely an obvious adaptation (illustrated by Kneller and comparisons between prior failed inventions and later successful ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty regarding recording of assignments and effect on action
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof may be given at trial of the recording of an assignment either before or after the action was brought; omission to aver recording may be cured by verdict if the declaration otherwise permitted proof of the recording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording is essential to pass title by assignment under certain statutes; courts will allow proof of recording at trial and will presume necessary facts after verdict if pleadings otherwise permitted the evidence.
